title: Audio guide
recordedFor: Twelve short listens, recorded for revision 7 of the collection.
gap: Now covers hunger and thirst, no fast travel by the map, job boards, vampire attacks and the optional gear mods.

episodes.title: Welcome: what our mods change
episodes.summary: The map of the whole series: which mods are installed, what installed does and does not promise, and which episodes to hear next.
transcript: Welcome. This is the first of a series of short listens about how our Skyrim differs from the Skyrim you remember. This one is the map: what is installed, what that does and does not promise, and which episodes to listen to next.

First, what counts. Everything on this list is installed in our game. Installed means a mod is present and switched on. It does not mean every feature has been tried with a full party. At the time of recording, the group has not yet played this exact setup together. So whenever you hear the words "not yet tested in multiplayer", that is the honest state of things today.
Here is the whole list, grouped by job.

For multiplayer and support, there is Skyrim Together Reborn, now at version one point eight point three, the Skyrim Script Extender, and Address Library. Skyrim Together is the one that turns a single-player game into a shared world. The other two work quietly behind it.
For combat and movement, there are Mortal Enemies, Precision, and True Directional Movement. They change how enemies swing, how your weapon connects, and how your character moves and locks on.

For magic, perks and races, there are Mysticism, Better Vanilla Perks, and Imperious. Mysticism reworks the spells. Better Vanilla Perks reworks what each perk gives you. Imperious replaces what each race gets. New in revision seven is a small patch of our own that gives two of those races a racial power back, and episode five explains it.
For the start of the game, there is Helgen Express. It swaps the long cart ride for a quick start screen.

For menus and settings, there are SkyUI, Skyrim Souls, MCM Helper and Display Tweaks. SkyUI gives you sortable inventory and magic menus. Skyrim Souls is the one to remember: menus no longer pause the world.
For information on screen, there are TrueHUD, which puts health bars over enemies, and moreHUD, which tells you more about the things you look at.
For looting and interaction, there are QuickLoot and Better Third Person Selection. Both make picking things up faster.

For the map, there is Atlas Map Markers, which adds hundreds of missing markers. Alongside it, Disable Fast Travel switches off fast travel by clicking the map. You get there on foot, or by carriage or ferry. Carriages and ferries should still work, but that has not been tested yet.

And three more are new in revision seven, and they change the feel of the world. Random Dragons No More switches off the random dragon attacks, while story dragons and dragons placed in the world are meant to remain. Cathedral Weathers and Seasons brings moodier weather, fog, thunder and darker nights. And Sounds of Skyrim Complete, with a small patch so it works alongside the weather, adds ambient sound in the wild, in caves, in ruins and at night.
For hunger and thirst, there is Simplest Survival, with Keyword Item Distributor to mark which items count as food and drink, and a small patch of our own that sets the timing.

For jobs and danger, there is The Notice Board, which puts job boards outside inns, and Vampire Attacks Restored, which brings back vampire attacks at night. A small patch of our own keeps those attacks away until level twelve.

Last, three optional mods add gear. They are Playable Greybeard Robes, Wizard Hats, and a Lord of the Rings weapon collection. Each player chooses whether to install them, and without them you will not see that gear on your friends.

That is the whole list. Every feature in this series comes from it. There is no perk overhaul other than Better Vanilla Perks, and no spell pack other than Mysticism. If a video or a website shows something we do not have, it does not apply to our game.
Now, which episodes are for you.

Episodes one to five are for everyone. This is episode one. Episode two is joining and leaving: setting up once, starting offline, connecting, and leaving properly. Episode three is playing as a party: the leader, saves, going down, shared experience, what is and is not shared, and the full list of features we are holding back until they are tested. Episode four is fighting in our Skyrim. Episode five is races and your racial power, which matters most before you create a character.

After those five, pick the path that matches how you want to play. If you will fight with blades, shields and armor, episode six is yours. If you will cast, episode seven covers attack and control, and episode eight covers healing and summoning. Healers and summoners can start with eight. If you will sneak, shoot a bow, pick locks or talk your way through, episode nine is the stealth path.
Episodes ten to twelve help everyone, but they can wait until after your first night. Ten is inventory, looting and a home. Eleven is builds off the beaten path. Twelve is what to go looking for.
You do not have to listen to everything. The first five give you enough to join in and stay out of trouble, and the rest are there when you want them.
That is the end of episode one.

episodes.title: Joining and leaving
episodes.summary: The one-time setup, connecting to the host, getting through a night, and leaving without losing progress.
transcript: This is episode two, for everyone: how to get into the host's game, how to get through a night, and how to leave without losing progress.
Start with the one-time setup.

First, your game has to match. Install revision seven of the collection, using the setup guide that comes with it, and start the game from your Skyrim Together shortcut rather than the ordinary Skyrim launcher. If the game ever tells you the server has a different version of Skyrim Together, don't fiddle. Tell the host.

Second, Tailscale. This is how you reach the host's computer. Tailscale is an app that makes a private, encrypted connection between devices, and a free personal account is enough. The host shares one computer with you. Once you accept, your computer can reach that one computer and nothing else of theirs. It only goes one way: the host's computer can answer yours, but it cannot start connections to your devices. Your normal internet traffic does not go through Tailscale or through the host. You do not open ports or change any router settings.

Install it from Tailscale's own website. Windows asks once for permission. Check that the publisher says Tailscale Inc., then say yes. A small Tailscale icon appears near the clock. Right-click it and log in with a personal Google, Microsoft, Apple or GitHub account, not a work or school one. If it asks whether this is for business or personal use, pick personal.

Then open the share link the host sends you privately, and accept it with the same account you just used. Treat that link like a password. Now right-click the Tailscale icon, open Network devices, and you should see the host's computer listed. Unused links stop working after thirty days, so if the page says the invitation is no longer valid, ask the host for a new one.

Next, the offline start. Our start of the game is Helgen Express, which replaces the long cart ride and the execution with a start screen. You click through tabs to choose your race, your starting standing stone, your armor, your weapon, your spells and who helps you escape, and then you click Ready. Do all of that offline, before you connect, and make a save once you are out of the introduction. Choose your race with care, because episode five is about what each race really gets.

Now, joining. Check that Tailscale is running, start the game from your Skyrim Together shortcut, press Right Control or F two, and click Connect. You will see an Address box and a Password box. The host sends you the address and the password privately, along with exactly what to type, so nothing is read out here. Type them in and click Connect. You should hear a confirmation and see the words "Successfully connected to server" in the small chat window.

If instead you see "Could not connect to the specified server", check three things. Is Tailscale running? It stops when you sign out of Windows or restart. Did you sign in with the same account that accepted the share? If not, right-click the icon, choose the account that accepted it, or add it. And did the share go through? If the host's computer is not in Network devices, open the link again. A Windows note saying there is no internet access on the Tailscale network is harmless.

Now, during the night. As the server is set, everyone who connects joins the one party automatically, and one game day lasts about seventy-two real minutes. The server runs the clock, so nobody can sleep or wait time forward. Your save lives on your own computer, so save at safe moments, not only at the end. Episode three covers the rest of party life.

Last, leaving. It is two steps: save, then quit. Let the save finish. Then use Quit to Main Menu, which works properly under Skyrim Together. If you go on to exit the program itself, expect it to crash at the very end. That happens on both version one point eight point two and one point eight point three. It happens after your save is written, and it is harmless apart from leaving a crash file behind. So there is no need to worry about it.
If you have to leave in a hurry, the steps are the same, just quicker. Save if you can, let it finish, then quit.
If you want Tailscale off between nights, right-click its icon and choose disconnect. Just remember to check it is running before the next one.
That is the end of episode two.

episodes.title: Playing as a party
episodes.summary: Who leads, what is shared and what stays yours, what falling down means now, and the features quarantined until they are tested.
transcript: This is episode three, for everyone. It is about what changes when several people share one Skyrim: who leads, what is shared, what stays yours, and what falling down means now. Episode four takes the fighting itself.

Start with the shared world. In ordinary Skyrim the world exists for you alone. It waits while you read, and it reloads when you die. Under Skyrim Together, other players' characters travel the same roads and fight the same enemies as you. Enemies, their equipment, and the contents of chests are shared between our games.

Quests come first. One player is the party leader, and for our campaign it stays the same person the whole way through. When the leader's quest moves forward, the server copies that progress to everyone, so all your journals move together. Only the leader should talk to quest characters and pick up quest items. Everyone can talk a choice over, but the leader makes it in the dialogue. Everyone else should keep their hands off quest actions, because in the version we run, the server does not check who made a quest change. If someone starts a quest by accident, that is fine, as long as they do not advance it before the leader has started it too. If a quest gets stuck, the leader can use the quest debugger, but Skyrim Together's own guide warns that it can skip the quest entirely. As the server is set, miscellaneous quests are not shared at all. Anyone who does one does it alone, and only they get the result. The Notice Board puts job boards outside inns, and most of its jobs are the miscellaneous kind. So the leader takes a job and everyone goes along, but the others will probably not see it in their journals. Who gets the reward has not been tested.

What about quest rewards? We do not know yet. Journal entries are copied from the leader. Who receives the gold or items a quest hands out has not been tested, and it may depend on whether the reward comes from a quest step or from a conversation. We will watch the first hand-in. And Skyrim gives no experience for finishing a quest anyway. You level by using skills.

If the leader's game drops, our reading of the code says leadership passes to whoever is next on the list, and Skyrim Together's own guide warns that changing leaders can break current quests. So agree beforehand who would take over.

Now saving. Each player keeps their own saves on their own computer. The server does not store your character, so save before the session ends. Use one character per campaign. If some of you want a solo game or a smaller group game, make a separate character, so the group characters do not move ahead while someone is away.

Next, going down. As the server is set, the death system is on, and it takes no gold. When you fall, the screen fades, and about five seconds later you get back up at full health. Outdoors that is nearby, and inside a dungeon it is the entrance. Then you cannot be hurt for about ten seconds. You lose no items, and there is no reload. Dying also pays off all your bounties at once. That is handy if it happens by accident and a loophole if it happens on purpose, so agree not to use it. As for helping a fallen friend, we found no way for a healer to stand someone back up. That is our reading of the code, not something we have watched.

As the server is set, experience is shared for combat. When anyone gains experience in a combat skill, everyone else gains the same amount in whichever combat skill they last used. The combat skills here are One-handed, Two-handed, Archery, Block, and the schools of Alteration, Conjuration, Destruction, Illusion and Restoration. Nothing else is shared. Smithing, alchemy and enchanting level only for whoever is doing the crafting, and the armor, stealth and speech skills level only for their own user. Whether every skill gains exactly as it would alone, especially when you heal a friend, is not yet tested in multiplayer.

Difficulty. As the server is set, everyone plays on Master, and Skyrim Together enforces the server's difficulty on every player while connected. Master means enemies take half the damage you deal, and you take double what they deal. It does not give enemies more health, and it does not add enemies or strengthen them because more players joined. By our arithmetic, a whole party fighting together faces roughly the pressure one person faces on the default setting, while someone tanking alone feels like a hard single-player game. That is arithmetic, not something we have watched.

As the server is set, friendly fire is off: player damage between us is switched off. Followers, guards and townspeople are not players, though. They can still be hit, and they will still take offence.

Now loot, gold and supplies. Gold is personal. Everyone has their own purse and nothing is pooled. Chests and bodies in the world are one shared pile, so as far as we can tell, loot goes to whoever grabs it, not to everyone at once. Nobody has watched that in our exact setup yet, so agree who takes what. Whether you share one shopkeeper's gold, or each see your own, has not been confirmed. As the server is set, dropped items are not shared, and chests in homes are private to each player. There is also no trading window, so handing something over means a shared chest out in the world, not one in a house. Episode ten goes into homes and handing things over. Crafted potions and enchanted gear are untested for hand-overs, so craft for yourself, and pass raw ingredients and ore for now. Everyone drinks from their own pack, so a party burns a party's worth of potions, and on Master you will probably drink more. Our setup does add hunger and thirst, from Simplest Survival. About thirty real minutes after you last ate, Hunger sets in, and about thirty after you last drank, Thirst does. Each one halves your health, magicka and stamina regeneration. Eating food clears Hunger, and drinking a potion clears Thirst. The clock starts the first time you eat or drink. Nothing in our setup adds cold.

Chat and short calls help when nobody can pause. Typing in the small chat window works, so nobody needs a microphone. A few calls are worth agreeing. "Menu" means you need a safe moment. "Leader talking" means let the conversation finish. "On me" means an enemy is chasing you and you are coming back toward the group. "Ready" means everyone has a target and a place to fall back to.
Finally, the one place we keep the whole list of features the group is holding back until they have been tested together. Later episodes mention only the ones in their own skills.

From Mysticism, we hold Mark and Recall, and everything that raises a corpse, including those scrolls and staves. From Better Vanilla Perks, we hold the second rank of Strong Reflexes. We hold the first rank of Steady Hand and the rest of that branch. We hold the second rank of Dark Souls, which makes raised bodies explode, and the fourth and fifth ranks of Dragonborn in Speech, which bring a spectral drum and a Dremora merchant. We hold the torch method of unlocking, so pick locks by hand, and we allow only one summon per player. Do not count on the Resurgence perk to boost healing, because its bonus is not confirmed. From Imperious, we hold Contingency, Beast Tongue, Spirit Walk and Red Sand Dance. Held means do not use it in the group until it has been tested.
That is the end of episode three.

episodes.title: Fighting in our Skyrim
episodes.summary: What a fight feels like: enemies that commit to their swings, free-turning movement with lock-on, real weapon hitboxes, and Master difficulty.
transcript: This is episode four, for everyone: what a fight feels like in our Skyrim. Episode three explained that the server is set to Master, and that is the backdrop for everything here.

Start with the enemies, because you will notice them first. In ordinary Skyrim, an enemy who starts a swing can keep turning while the attack plays out. You step to the side and the axe follows you round. Mortal Enemies changes that. Enemies commit to a swing once it starts, and they cannot spin all the way around in the middle of it. So the wind-up is worth watching. You see a draugr raise its sword, you step aside, the blow lands where you were, and now you have a moment to hit back. Sidestep and punish becomes a real pattern. It does not make enemies weaker, and on Master a committed blow that lands still hurts. Whether the timing looks the same on every player's screen is not yet tested in multiplayer, so learn it together on the first night.

Next, how you move. In ordinary Skyrim, third person movement is tied tightly to the camera. With True Directional Movement, your character turns and runs in whatever direction you press, while the camera stays free. You can run toward the camera, circle an enemy and back away naturally.

It also adds target lock. Press the middle mouse button to lock onto an enemy. A marker appears on the target, and your character keeps facing it. Scroll the mouse wheel to switch to another enemy, and press the middle button again to let go. Our setting only locks onto hostile targets. You can never lock onto a friend, so nobody fixes their camera on a teammate in a chaotic fight. It also means a healer cannot use lock-on to aim a heal. Healing a friend means aiming by hand.

Then, health bars, from TrueHUD. It puts health bars over the enemies in the fight, adds a large boss bar for important opponents, and shows target information when you lock on. In a group that is quietly useful, because everyone can see which enemy is nearly finished. Whether TrueHUD reliably shows the health of other players is not yet tested in multiplayer, so do not count on it to tell you a friend needs healing. Listen for them instead.

Now the rhythm of a fight. Skyrim Souls means menus no longer pause the game. If you open your bag in the middle of a fight, an enemy can still hit you, and your friends are not frozen by your menus. Step back, or call out "menu", before you browse. Put your potions and spells in your favourites before you go into a dungeon.

Your own weapon is changed by Precision, which decides hits by where the blade or hammer actually travels. A wide sideways swing can catch two or three enemies in one pass, and a thrust that misses on screen misses in the game. Episode six covers that in depth for melee players, but two points matter to everyone. The first is spacing. Big weapons sweep a real arc, so a frontliner needs room, and friends should not stand right beside a swing. As the server is set, player damage is off, so you will not hurt each other, but the swing still has to travel somewhere. The second is the people who are not players. Followers, guards and townspeople can still be struck, and hitting one still makes them angry, which is easier to do by accident in a crowded room. Older reports from other players say hit reactions can look different on another person's screen. How that looks across our connected games is not yet tested in multiplayer.
One thing to know about kill cams. Kill cams may appear when you are not connected. We have not confirmed how they behave once you are connected, so do not be surprised either way.
Now some changes that are new in our game, and they all touch fights.

First, dragons. In ordinary Skyrim, once the story gets going, random dragon attacks can happen every few game days as you travel. Random Dragons No More switches those off. Story dragons and dragons placed in the world are meant to remain. We checked the mod's file, and its off switch is locked, so the game's own quest should not turn random attacks back on. Skyrim Together's own documentation says some random encounters may not appear in everyone's world, which is a good reason not to have them. The mod is still being tested, so we have not yet watched a play session with it.

Second, the weather. Cathedral Weathers and Seasons brings moodier skies, fog, thunder and darker nights. Expect it to be harder to see what is coming. Weather in Skyrim Together is decided by the party leader's game, so everyone should see the same sky. It is not yet tested in multiplayer with our group.

Third, the sound. Sounds of Skyrim Complete adds ambient sound: wolves and ravens at night, dripping and echoing caves, moaning undead in draugr dungeons, and screams from the Falmer. In ruins and caves you may hear trouble before you see it. The sounds play on your own computer, so nothing needs to sync between players.

Fourth, vampires. Vampire Attacks Restored brings back vampire attacks on towns and villages at night, outside the walled cities, and a guard has to be present. A small patch of our own keeps them away until level twelve. Until level thirty they are less likely, and they become more likely as you level up. Random encounters may not appear for everyone, so how an attack looks for each player is not yet tested in multiplayer.

So, put together. Enemies commit to their swings, so you can dodge them. You move freely and lock onto the dangerous enemy, never a friend. Health bars show which target is nearly done. Menus do not pause, so prepare before the dungeon. Random dragons are meant to be off, vampires may attack towns at night, and the world is darker and louder. And when you fall, as episode three said, you get back up and rejoin your friends.
That is the end of episode four.

episodes.title: Races and your racial power
episodes.summary: How Imperious replaces the usual race bonuses, what earning a racial power asks of you, and our small patch that gives two races a power back.
transcript: This is episode five of our series on what our mods change. It is for anyone choosing a character, and it finishes the group of episodes that everyone should hear.

Start with the ordinary game. Every race begins with a few passive advantages and one power you can use from the first minute. Nords resist frost. Bretons resist magic. Khajiit have claws and night vision.

Imperious is the mod that changes this, and it replaces that package rather than adding to it. Each race gets a new set of passive abilities, and most of them come with real tradeoffs. Each race also has a power that you earn by reaching a racial goal during play, instead of having it from the start. The familiar bonus does not simply stay on top. Nords are the clearest example. In the ordinary game they resist half of frost damage. Here they resist a quarter, and they gain other things, such as hitting harder as they get badly hurt.

You choose your race on the Helgen Express start screen, before you connect. Your powers then appear in the Magic menu, under Powers. Any race can learn any skill, so a Wood Elf can be a healer and an Orc can be a mage. Race gives you flavor and a few edges. It does not lock you into a class. And the characters of each race out in the world get these changes too, not only players.

One more thing before the tour. The mod also reshuffles starting health, magicka, stamina and carrying capacity. As the mod describes it, High Elves start with the highest magicka but the lowest carrying capacity, and Orcs start with the most stamina and the highest capacity, but the least magicka.
Now the ten races, with what each one gains and what each one loses.

High Elves become enchanters. Their enchantments are fifteen percent stronger, but their weapons and armor are fifteen percent weaker. They recover magicka and stamina faster when either one drops below half, at some cost to their defenses. Their starting magicka is lower than in the ordinary game. A High Elf makes a good mage or spellblade, but an early pure caster feels the lost defense.

Argonians swim twice as fast and keep waterbreathing. They also recover from the brink, getting resources back when they run very low. Their earned power is Caustic Spit, a strong spit that weakens an enemy's armor and magic resistance, and you earn it by finding four underwater chests. They lose the ordinary Argonian healing power and the disease resistance. This race suits explorers and mobile support.

Wood Elves become hunters. Their Harrier ability marks prey, and they can sense movement while standing still and sneaking. They can also eat from corpses to gain temporary resources. They lose their ordinary animal-command power and their resistance to poison and disease. They make natural scouts.

Bretons lose some magic resistance. It drops from twenty-five percent to fifteen, and Dragonskin is gone. In exchange they gain extra effects from standing stones, and spell absorption that switches on when their magicka runs low. After you discover ten standing stones, the Breton ability called Shared Ancestry lets a Breton borrow another race's power for five minutes. That sounds wonderful, but it comes with a catch that we will get to in a moment.

Dark Elves draw on their ancestors. They can spend favor to call on a guardian that gives them extra armor for two minutes, and they gain favor from marked kills. They resist fire by twenty-five percent instead of fifty. The ordinary fire cloak is gone.

Imperials get an aura that gives nearby allies bonuses to armor and attack. They also recover some combat resource faster, and they make a choice at levels ten, twenty and thirty. After twenty quests they earn a refill of magicka and stamina. They lose the ordinary power that calms a crowd. An Imperial suits a party face or a guardian.

Khajiit move fifteen percent faster, and they sneak more quietly, with a stamina-powered leap called Prowl. Their claws are weaker than before. A plain claw strike does ten damage, down from twenty-two, but power attacks scale with stamina. The ordinary night vision is gone until you earn its replacement by collecting fifty thousand gold over your lifetime.

Nords, as we said, resist frost by a quarter. They choose favored enemy races at levels ten, twenty and thirty. After clearing eight dungeons they earn a half-minute of very fast magicka and stamina recovery, and during it their frost resistance climbs to three quarters. They lose Battle Cry.

Orcs get a burst of speed and resources at the start of a fight, and a jump that staggers enemies once per battle. Their weapons and armor are twenty percent better, and their enchantments are twenty percent worse. After staggering enemies with that jump a hundred and fifty times, they earn Berserk, which doubles attack and critical damage and halves spell costs for fifteen seconds. The ordinary minute of Berserker Rage is gone, and Berserk does not give back its protection.

Redguards build momentum from humanoid kills, with a short boost to damage, critical hits and costs. They never run out of stamina outside combat, and they recover faster as their health falls. Imperious takes away their ordinary Adrenaline Rush power and their poison resistance, though they gain fifty percent resistance to disease. More on that power in a moment.
Now the part that matters most, which is the powers.

As episode three explained, some features are held. Held means we are not using the feature until it has been tested with a group. Four of the earned racial powers are held. Contingency for High Elves, which casts stored spells for you. Red Sand Dance for Redguards, which slows time. Beast Tongue for Wood Elves, which recruits an animal companion. And Spirit Walk for Dark Elves, which summons ancestors. That is also the catch with Shared Ancestry. A Breton cannot borrow a held power, so those four stay off limits there too.

Imperious removed the original power of every race, and for four races the replacement is held. That left High Elves, Redguards, Wood Elves and Dark Elves with no racial power they were permitted to use. For revision seven, we made a small patch of our own. It gives High Elves their Highborn power back, and it gives Redguards their Adrenaline Rush back. In the ordinary game, Highborn was a once-a-day burst of faster magicka recovery, and Adrenaline Rush was a once-a-day burst of faster stamina recovery. We tested the patch in the game, in single-player. Both powers appeared and could be cast. They locked out for the rest of the day after use, and they survived saving and loading. Test characters made before the patch picked them up too. What we have not done is play them in a real fight, and we have not tested them in multiplayer. The patch gives back only the power. It does not give back the Redguard's poison resistance.

Dark Elves and Wood Elves are different. They still have no permitted racial power. Candidate patches for them exist, but they are not part of this revision. So if you pick a Dark Elf or a Wood Elf, you keep the passive abilities, but you will not use a racial power.

As episode one said, installed does not mean tested together. Several racial effects have not been tested in multiplayer at all. We do not yet know whether the Imperial aura reaches other players, or how Prowl and Harrier behave for friends.

So choose for the story you want. A High Elf can be a mage. A Khajiit or a Wood Elf makes a scout. A Nord or an Orc fits a fighter, an Argonian an explorer, and an Imperial the one who speaks for the group. Race helps, but you can learn every skill.
The races each have goals that unlock their power, and we cover those in a later episode. The next episodes follow the three paths, starting with the fighter's.

episodes.title: The combat path: blades, shields and armor
episodes.summary: For the melee fighter: One-handed, Two-handed, Block, Heavy Armor and Smithing, and how our fighting mods change them.
transcript: This is episode six of our series on what our mods change. It is for the melee fighter, and it covers One-handed, Two-handed, Block, Heavy Armor and Smithing. If you have heard episodes one to five, you are ready for it. As episode five said, Orcs and Nords suit this path, though any race can learn any skill.

Three mods shape a fight, and episode four introduced them. Here is how they land on a fighter. As episode four said, Mortal Enemies makes enemies commit to their swings. For you, that commitment is the opening. You watch the wind-up, you step aside or raise your shield, and the blow arrives where you used to be. Then you hit back.

The second reminder is about difficulty. As episode three said, the server is set to Master. Enemies take half of the damage you deal, and you take double the damage they deal. That is why the opening matters so much, and why a fighter who simply trades blows will not enjoy the night. By simple arithmetic, a party that is all fighting at once faces about the same pressure as one person on the ordinary difficulty, while a lone fighter has to absorb about four times as much damage to win the same fight. That is arithmetic, not something we have watched happen, but it points the same way. Fight together, and keep your health up.
Now Precision, which is the biggest change to your own weapon, so it deserves some time.

In the ordinary game, a melee hit lands if the enemy is roughly in front of you and roughly in reach, whatever the blade did on screen. Precision follows the weapon itself. The hit is decided by where the blade or the hammer actually travels. Three things matter, and they are reach, angle and spacing.

Reach first. The length of your weapon counts. A long weapon touches things a short one cannot, and a thrust that misses on screen misses in the game. Angle second. A wide sideways swing can catch two or three enemies in one pass, but a swing from a bad angle can slide right past a target that looked close enough. Spacing third. A good fighter keeps enemies at the distance where the weapon works best, and keeps friends out of the arc.
There is also a little feedback when you connect. You get a very short pause on impact and a small camera shake, so a solid hit feels solid. That is the mod telling you the blow landed.

Spacing has a second side, which is friends. As the server is set, player damage between friends is switched off, so you cannot hurt each other. But the swing still has to go somewhere. Two-handed weapons sweep a real arc, so a fighter with a big weapon needs room, and friends should not stand right beside a big swing. Followers, guards and townspeople can still be struck, and hitting one still makes them angry. Precision makes that easier to do by accident in a crowded room. So take care in a town, and think about the arc before you swing in a doorway.
Older community reports say hit reactions can look different on another player's screen. Whether our connected games match is not yet tested in multiplayer.

Now the perks, which come from Better Vanilla Perks. It keeps the familiar trees and their shape, but it rewrites many of the perks. Familiar names may now do different things, so read each description before you spend a point.

For One-handed, the first perk, Armsman, still raises your damage, and it now adds critical chance as well. One-handed fighters usually carry a shield or a spell in the other hand. Those are very different setups. A sword and shield makes you hard to hurt. A sword and a spell gives you more options but leaves you open, because casting creates a gap in your defense. Swapping hands in the middle of a fight also creates a gap, so decide in advance what your off hand will do.

For Two-handed, you get heavy attacks and the ability to block with your weapon. The perks that belong to shields do not apply to a two-handed fighter, so do not expect shield protection from a greatsword. In return you get weight behind every swing, and the sweeping arc we described. Two-handed fighters have to swap weapons to heal or to summon, so a friend who covers you while you do it is worth a great deal.

Block is the skill for standing between danger and a friend. It gives you defense, bashes and interruption. Health comes first for a blocker, with stamina next, because stamina pays for blocking, bashing and backing away. Be clear about one thing, though. A tank has no guaranteed taunt. Enemies do not have to stay on you just because you are big and shiny. So a blocker's job is not to hold every enemy's attention. It is to be the sturdy one, to bash a useful opening, and to give friends room to work.

Here is where the group rules matter. Strong Reflexes rank one, at Block thirty, halves the damage you take from power attacks while you block with a shield. That rank is allowed, and it is a fine choice. Strong Reflexes rank two, at Block fifty, slows time when you block a power attack. We are holding that rank. Skyrim Together does support slow time, but it has not been tested with this perk, so we have set it aside until it is. Held means we are not using it until a group has tested it. If you reach Block fifty, look at your other options instead. Armor and weapon perks give you plenty to buy.

Heavy Armor is physical protection, and it suits fighters and anyone who stands near the front. One change helps with looks. Heavy Armor and Light Armor set bonuses can work with three matching pieces instead of four, which gives you freedom over your helmet. Armor is a choice, not a class rule. Start with one approach, and avoid spreading your perks across every armor tree. Improve your weapon and your armor before you invest deeply in crafting.

Smithing is the skill for forging and improving equipment. Better Vanilla Perks gives each material its own perk. That perk lets you make the gear and, for most materials, improve it twice as much as before. A separate perk, Arcane Blacksmith, doubles the improvement of magical items, leather, hide and faction armor. The good news is that one fighter can become the party's weaponsmith. Skyrim Together shares experience for combat skills, as episode three said, but crafting such as smithing levels only for the person at the forge. So a dedicated smith levels fastest.

Here is the honest limit. We have not confirmed that gear you improved keeps its improvements when you hand it to a friend. So craft for yourself, and share the materials. If you want to give a friend something finished, test it with one item first.

One optional extra. A Lord of the Rings weapon collection mod adds weapons you can craft, including swords and axes. It is optional, so ask who has it. A friend without the mod will not see those weapons on you, and handing one over is untested.

One option is worth a mention. If you want a guardian rather than a bruiser, choose One-handed with a shield from the start instead of Two-handed. You keep your armor and your ability to interrupt, without paying for two weapon trees.

Put together, a fighter in our game fights like this. Choose one armor approach and one weapon setup. Fight at a corner, with space behind you. Block or sidestep, bash an opening if there is one, attack, and reset. Keep friends out of your swing.

A simple rhythm helps in the first room of any dungeon. Look, agree on a target and a retreat corner, open the fight, focus on one enemy at a time, recover, and reset. Short calls keep it smooth. Ready, on me, and cover my cast are all you need. A friend who calls on me is being chased and should come back toward you, and the rest of the party steps in to intercept.
And remember the menus. Because menus do not pause the game, set up your favorites before the dungeon, not during it.
That is the fighter's path. The next episodes follow the other paths, beginning with the magic path.

episodes.title: The magic path, part one: attack and control
episodes.summary: For casters: Destruction, Alteration, Illusion and Enchanting, and how Mysticism reworks the spell lists.
transcript: This is episode seven of our series on what our mods change. It is for casters, and it covers Destruction, Alteration, Illusion and Enchanting. Healing and summoning have their own episode, which is the next one. You only need episodes one to five to follow this one.
Everything here starts with Mysticism, the mod that reworks spells.

The ordinary game has five schools of magic, with a fairly short list of spells in each. Mysticism keeps the five schools, but it reworks the whole selection. Familiar spells are rebalanced, and many new spells are added in every school. A few spells move to a different school. By one count, the mod teaches nearly three hundred spells from tomes. You still learn them the usual way, from spell tomes and from the usual vendors. There is no new skill called Mysticism. It changes what is inside the schools you already know, and it gives spells better scaling.
Here is a tour of the schools in this episode, with some examples.

Destruction first. Besides the fire, frost and shock you know, it gains more ways to drain an enemy, including Vampiric Touch and Vampiric Bolt, which steal health. Keep a second damage type in your pocket. Some enemies resist fire or frost, and a destruction mage who has only one answer will have a bad time against them.

Alteration gains practical tools. Feather lets you carry more, and Corrode Armor weakens an enemy's protection. The school is about personal protection, utility and weakening enemies. A debuff like Corrode Armor, or Weakness to Fire, can set up a friend's damage, but whether those effects reach a friend's game the way you expect has not been confirmed.

Illusion is the school of control. One change here is that Paralysis moves out of Alteration and into Illusion, so a control caster looks for it in this school. Illusion also has morale magic, such as Courage, Rally and Call to Arms. Skyrim Together has code to pass those effects between players, but how they work in our modded party has not been confirmed. And remember that some enemies resist control. If you have paralyzed or calmed an enemy on purpose, tell your friends. A short call such as, leave that one, keeps them from undoing your work.
Enchanting works in a different way, and we will get to it in a moment.
Now the part that matters most for casters, because it is a real file conflict and not just a description.

Mysticism and Better Vanilla Perks both edit some of the same spells. When two mods change the same thing, the one loaded later wins. In our setup, Better Vanilla Perks loads after Mysticism, and it wins on eighteen shared records. So if you read Mysticism's own page, some of what it says about these spells may not hold in our game. This combination has mixed behavior, and descriptions based on Mysticism alone can be wrong.

Here is what it means in practice, and the first point is the one people get wrong. The spells you learn from tomes are not hurt. Flames keeps Mysticism's three effects, which are its damage, a fear effect that depends on the matching perk and target, and an extra burning effect. Frostbite keeps its three. It damages health and stamina, it slows the target, and it has a conditional Deep Freeze effect that paralyzes. Sparks keeps its two, which are damage and a conditional Disintegrate effect. This holds in either load order, and those conditional effects still depend on the relevant perks and targets.

So where did the conflict land? On the enemy versions. Enemy spellcasters use their own hand-held copies of these three spells, and in those copies Better Vanilla Perks wins. Those versions lose some of the extra effects, or use different casting settings. That affects the enemies' spells, not yours. In plain terms, you keep the full spell. The enemy mage gets a plainer one.
The one change that you will notice is Candlelight. It lasts one hundred and twenty seconds instead of Mysticism's three hundred. That is true for the spell and for the scroll.

This revision also adds a weather mod, Cathedral Weathers and Seasons, which brings moodier weather, fog, thunder and darker nights. If a night gets dark enough that you cannot see, a light spell may be handy, even a shorter one. The mod's page says it has its own setting for how bright the night is, so each player should be able to adjust it for themselves. We have not yet played that combination, so take it as something to try.

One more caution. This is what the files say. We have read the records, but we have not measured the results in a fight. The spell menu is not proof either. Text in a menu describes what the designer meant, and it can disagree with what the spell stores underneath. Stendarr's Aura is a good example. Its menu says ten damage, while the damage spell underneath stores eight, and we do not know the real number. So treat numbers on the screen as a hint, not a promise.

One more thing about the two mods. They do not fight over perks. There are no perk records that both of them change, so Mysticism does not take any perks away from you. The effect of the load order is on spells, effects and creatures, not on the perk trees.

Now perks, which come from Better Vanilla Perks. It keeps the same eighteen skill trees and the same overall shape, but it rewrites what many perks do. A familiar perk name may do something different now. Read each description before you spend a point, and do not trust an old guide. We have not catalogued every Destruction, Alteration and Illusion perk here, so the in-game description is your best source.

Enchanting has clearer perk changes. The Enchanter perks make new enchantments stronger, from twenty percent at the first rank up to one hundred percent at the top, and they let you recharge weapons from slain souls. Fire Enchanter, Storm Enchanter and Corpus Enchanter boost particular kinds of enchantment. As episode five said, race matters here as well. High Elves have enchantments that are fifteen percent stronger, and Orcs have enchantments that are twenty percent weaker, so a High Elf enchanter has a head start.

There are two honest limits on Enchanting. First, enchanting levels only for the person who does the enchanting, because Skyrim Together shares experience for combat skills, not crafting. So it suits a specialist, and one dedicated enchanter levels fastest. Second, we have not confirmed that a custom enchantment survives being handed to a friend. Reports disagree about whether the item arrives with its enchantment or as the plain item. So enchant for yourself first, and test one item before you build a supply chain on it.

A few habits for all casters. Hand-cast spells train their school, but staffs do not normally train the school, and how staffs interact with the changed perks has not been confirmed. If you rely on a staff, carry charged soul gems. Set your favorites before the dungeon, because menus do not pause the game, as episode four said. And remember that player damage between friends is switched off, as the server is set and as episode three explained. A lightning bolt will not hurt a friend, though followers, guards and townspeople still need care.

A word on looks. Two optional mods suit casters. Wizard Hats adds craftable hats in many colors, and Playable Greybeard Robes adds a craftable robe, hood and boots. A friend without them will not see that gear on you.

Last, one Mysticism feature that casters should know about is held. Mark and Recall let you set a point and teleport back to it. They are Conjuration spells, so they come up again in the next episode. We are not using them until they have been tested with a group. The worry is that teleporting could split the party, or split its quest progress. That is a guess, not something we have seen, and nobody has found a specific failure. Until it is tested, we walk.

So the caster's path is a richer one than in the ordinary game. The spells you learn keep their full effects, enemy mages get plainer ones, and a few numbers, like Candlelight, are different from what you may expect. The next episode covers healing and summoning.

episodes.title: The magic path, part two: healing and summoning
episodes.summary: For healers and summoners: Restoration and Conjuration, where Better Vanilla Perks overrides Mysticism, and the one-summon limit.
transcript: This is episode eight of our series on what our mods change. It is for healers, for summoners, and for anyone who wants to help their friends with magic. It covers Restoration and Conjuration, and you only need episodes one to five to follow it. If you want attack and control magic, that was the last episode. As episode five said, any race can heal, so pick the one you like.

One thing to know before we start. The spells come from Mysticism, and the perks come from Better Vanilla Perks. Where those two mods change the same thing, the one loaded later wins, and in our game that is Better Vanilla Perks. We will see where that matters for summoners.
Start with healing, because Mysticism gives Restoration the most.

Heal Other becomes an Apprentice spell. That means you can heal a friend much earlier than in the ordinary game, once you have the tome. Close Greater Wounds is an area heal at Adept level. Breath of Life and Stendarr's Mercy are stronger area heals further on. Then there are circles that you place on the ground, called Circle of Life, Circle of Wisdom and Circle of Strength. They restore health, magicka or stamina around a spot, so they make a rally point. Whether those circles reach other players, and how long they last, has not been confirmed.

One change will trip people up. In the ordinary game, Grand Healing is a single burst that heals everyone near you. In Mysticism, Grand Healing is channeled, which means you hold the cast to keep the healing going. If a guide online calls it a burst, that guide is describing the ordinary game.

Does healing a friend work at all? The code of Skyrim Together has a path for healing another player, and healing spells that carry the restore health tag should reach other players. That is as far as we can say. We have not watched our group do it, so it is not yet tested in multiplayer. Custom buffs that are not healing are unverified.

Now aiming, which is the first thing a healer learns. As episode four said, lock-on in our game works on hostile targets only. You cannot lock onto a friend, so you aim a heal by hand. An area heal may be easier than tracking a friend who keeps moving. That is advice, not a measured result. It is also not yet tested whether the health bars show a friend's health reliably, so do not count on them. Listen for your friends instead. A short call, such as healing here, tells everyone where to retreat to.

Next, what a healer cannot do. As episode three said, the server is set with its death system on, so a player who falls goes down and gets back up, outdoors nearby, or at the entrance if you are inside, without losing gold. We found no way for a teammate's heal to stand a fallen friend back up. There is no resurrection spell for friends, and none is promised. We read that in the code and have not watched it. So think of the job this way. A healer keeps people from going down. A healer does not bring them back.

The healer's habits follow from that. Stand behind the frontline and a little to one side. Keep enough magicka for a rescue, and keep your food and potions handy, because Hunger and Thirst each cut your regeneration in half, magicka included. When everyone is healthy, reposition or add a little damage. Armor choice matters too, because some perks expect an unarmored outfit. And a healer needs cover. Call cover my cast, and let a friend step in while you heal.
Can a pure support character work? Yes, if the party provides damage and protects your casting space. Keep a defense, and keep something useful to do when nobody needs help.

Restoration also holds wards and anti-undead tools. A ward protects its caster. Whether it can protect a friend standing behind you has not been confirmed. Sun Fire, and Mysticism's Sunbeam, give you something to do against the undead.

Now the Better Vanilla Perks side of Restoration. Each of the cost-saving perks from Novice to Expert also adds a magicka regeneration effect that gets stronger as you climb. Master Restoration makes every Restoration spell half again as efficient. Then there is Resurgence. Its description says Restoration spells are thirty percent stronger. Do not lean on that yet. Skyrim Together handles that perk in its own way when you heal another player, and the real result has not been measured. The Necromage perk requires Resurgence, so if you want that branch, remember that we have not confirmed how the pieces behave. And we have not confirmed whether healing a friend trains your skill.
Now Conjuration, where the rules matter more.

Mysticism adds extra summons. You get a conjured skeleton and a skeleton archer. The familiar and atronach spells make good early helpers. Later, the Soul Cairn creatures, the Boneman, the Mistman and the Wrathman, become available. All of these are new conjured creatures. They are not corpses raised from the floor, and that difference is the point of the next part.

We keep one controlled summon per player. That is a budget we chose, not a limit of the game. Nobody has tested more helpers with four players, so we are holding there for now. A summoner who also heals has to budget magicka for a summon and for a rescue heal, and still keep enough health to survive. In practice, summon one helper, place it off to one side, and keep your escape lane clear. If calling a replacement would eat the magicka you need to heal, let the first one expire.

That budget changes how some Better Vanilla Perks work. Summoner and Puppeteer add range as well as capacity, so the range still helps you. Twin Souls only adds capacity, so it gives you nothing useful under one summon. Staff of the Atronach strengthens certain staffs and Conjuration spells, and lets potent atronachs scale with your level.

Which brings us to the load order conflict. Better Vanilla Perks wins on the creatures. The potent atronachs, and the creatures called by Mysticism's Monarch spells, use Better Vanilla Perks' creature definitions and its level scaling. Mysticism's own fixed levels and some of its extra creature abilities are not used. Those summon spells still last sixty seconds. How strong these creatures end up in a fight is something we have not measured, so call it a good bet and not a promise. Conjure Familiar, Poison Rune and Stendarr's Aura also use the perk mod's magic effects.

Last, the held features of this path, because a summoner should hear them together. Mark and Recall, which Mysticism files under Conjuration, are held, as episode three said. Corpse raising is held too. That means every spell, scroll and staff that raises a dead body, including Raise Zombie, Reanimate Corpse, Revenant, Dread Zombie and Dead Thrall. The Better Vanilla Perks rank called Dark Souls rank two, which makes raised bodies explode, is held with them. And extra summons beyond the one are held. Held means we are not using the feature until a group has tested it. A conjured skeleton is fine, because nobody had to raise a body.

So a supporter in our game has a lot to do, and the honest limit is that some of it has not been tried with four people. Learn the heals, aim by hand, summon one helper, and make your calls short. The next episodes follow the other paths.

episodes.title: The stealth path: sneak, bow and silver tongue
episodes.summary: For scouts, archers, thieves and talkers: Alchemy, Light Armor, Lockpicking, Pickpocket, Sneak, Speech and Archery, with three other players in the world.
transcript: This episode is for scouts, archers, thieves, potion makers and talkers. It makes sense if all you have heard is episodes one to five, and it is only about what our mods change for the stealth skills.

Skyrim's eighteen skills come in three groups of six. The stealth group is Alchemy, Light Armor, Lockpicking, Pickpocket, Sneak and Speech. Archery officially sits with the combat skills, but a stealth archer is the person who will go looking for it, so it belongs in this episode too.

Here is the first thing to know. Sneaking, shooting and picking pockets work the way you remember. What changes comes from three places: our perk overhaul, Better Vanilla Perks, which rewrites what many perks do; our racial overhaul, Imperious; and the simple fact that three other people are in the world with you.
Start with sneaking, because that is the scout's job.
According to the Skyrim Together wiki, the game's detection of fellow players is switched off. Your friends cannot spot you sneaking up behind them.

Here is what has not been tested in multiplayer. How enemies notice four people at once, whether sneak bonuses behave the way they do alone, and whether one player's detection helps another. So treat a scouting trip as an agreement among friends, not a guarantee. Scout only far enough to come back quickly. Name the dangerous target. Wait for someone to say ready before the first shot. And once the whole party charges in, stop expecting stealth to last. Keep moving and keep shooting.

Two short calls help a scout. "Ready" means the opening target is chosen and everyone knows where to fall back to. "On me" means you are being chased and running back toward the frontline, so the others can step in. These are suggestions for the table, not tested rules, but they cost nothing to try on the first night.

As episode four said, True Directional Movement only locks onto hostile targets. For a scout, that is a gift: you can lock onto the archer on the ledge, and your camera will never grab a friend by accident. TrueHUD, from the same episode, puts health bars over enemies, so everyone can see which one is nearly finished.
Next, your race, because Imperious touches stealth in a few places.

As episode five explained, Imperious replaces each race's original package rather than adding to it. For stealthy characters, here is what it offers. Khajiit move faster and sneak more quietly, and an ability called Prowl adds a leap that costs stamina. Wood Elves can detect movement while standing still in sneak, and they can mark their prey, which weakens its defense. Argonians sneak and move better after they have been swimming.

One honest limit. How these effects look to your friends, and whether the marking and Prowl reach the other players properly, has not been tested in multiplayer. One more point for Wood Elves. In revision seven, our own small patch gave High Elves and Redguards their racial power back, and we tested that in single-player on October fourth. Wood Elves, like Dark Elves, still have no racial power that the group permits. Their original power is gone, and Imperious's replacement is held.
Now Archery.

Better Vanilla Perks keeps the shape of the Archery tree but changes what the perks do, and it puts more weight on penetration and other offensive bow effects. Read each description before you spend a point.

There is one group rule here. In ordinary Skyrim, a perk at Archery forty slows time while you aim. Better Vanilla Perks keeps that idea in a perk called Steady Hand. Rank one, at Archery forty, slows time while you zoom with a bow, and it also adds critical chance. We are holding rank one until it has been tested with several players. Skyrim Together supports shared slow time, but nobody has watched this perk work in a group yet. Rank two, at Archery sixty, adds immunity to ranged disarming and better critical chance. It is held too, because it requires rank one. Everything else in the Archery tree is open to you, and there is plenty of it.
Archers get one more helper, the map. Atlas Map Markers adds hundreds of shrines, camps and landmarks, so you can report a route back to the group using real names.
Now Light Armor.

Light Armor is protected mobility. Better Vanilla Perks lets the set bonus work with three matching pieces instead of four, so you get to choose your helmet. Leave yourself room to move and to retreat. A light armor character is not meant to stand in the open and trade blows.
Now Lockpicking.

In our game you pick locks by hand. Better Vanilla Perks adds a torch trick, where holding a torch lets a perk open locks for you, and we are holding that until it has been tested. The five lock perks themselves still make manual picking easier, so they are well worth buying.
Now Pickpocket, and a short word about crime.

Crime is per person. A bounty belongs to the one who earned it, and ordinary shopkeepers will not buy stolen goods unless you have the Fence perk. The wiki lists pickpocketing another player as a feature that syncs, but what it does to anyone's bounty has not been confirmed in our setup, so do not practice on your friends. The wiki also says dying pays all of your bounties at once, which is handy by accident and a loophole if you use it on purpose. Agree as a group not to treat it as a plan. Finally, an old report on the Skyrim Together project's issue tracker said that when a party member opened ordinary containers, the party leader picked up small bounties. That report was closed, and nobody has confirmed whether it still happens, so watch the leader's bounty on your first visit to a town.
Now Alchemy.

Better Vanilla Perks makes alchemy more rewarding. The Alchemist perk raises the strength of potions and poisons in steps, up to twice as strong at the top, and ordinary weapons carry a free poison. Benefactor makes helpful potions stronger. Poisoner makes poisons stronger and makes doses last longer on melee weapons. Green Thumb gives you two ingredients from each plant you pick, and the plugin says it needs only seventy Alchemy. Whether picking a plant takes it away from your friends as well has not been confirmed.

The caution is about sharing. Alchemy experience only rises for the one who does the brewing, which suits a specialist. But handing finished potions to someone else has not been tested in multiplayer, and one open report on the Skyrim Together project's issue tracker says that player-made potions could not be shared. So brew for yourself, pass raw ingredients around, and test your first potion on a friend before you build a supply chain on it.
Last, Speech, the silver tongue.

As episode three said, the party leader drives quest conversations. Everyone can talk the choice through, but the leader picks the line. So Speech is mostly a trading skill, and a party face for flavor. In shops, anyone can use it.

Better Vanilla Perks gives Speech more than prices. The first Dragonborn rank improves your prices and gives one extra skill level every time you read a skill book. Merchant lets you sell any kind of item to any vendor. At Speech forty you gain the ability to breathe steam like a Dwarven Centurion, and that one has not been tested in multiplayer. The Dragonborn perks at Speech sixty and eighty give a spectral drum and a Dremora merchant. Both are held, so the early Speech perks are your toolkit for now.

Put together, the stealth path in our game looks like this. Scout briefly and come back. Shoot from the shadows, then keep moving, and leave Steady Hand alone for now. Wear light armor you can run in. Pick every lock by hand. Agree on crime before you commit it. Brew for yourself and pass around raw ingredients. And let your leader do the talking in quests while you make the money.
That is the end of the stealth path.

episodes.title: Inventory, looting and a home
episodes.summary: Menus that no longer pause the game, how looting works, what belongs to you in a shared world, and what to know before buying a house.
transcript: This episode is for everyone. It covers your menus, how looting works, what actually belongs to you in a shared world, and what to know about buying a house. It makes sense after episodes one to five, and it can wait until after your first night.
Start with the menus, because they are the first thing you will touch.

As episode four said, our menus do not pause the game. That comes from Skyrim Souls. In ordinary Skyrim, opening your inventory, the map, a book or the journal stops time. With Skyrim Souls, the world keeps running while you browse. Your friends are not frozen by your menus, and you are not safe inside them. If you open your bag in the middle of a fight, an enemy can still hit you. So step back before you browse, call out "menu" so your friends know you need a safe moment, and put your potions and spells in your favorites before you go into a dungeon.

SkyUI replaces the inventory, magic, barter and container menus. You get category tabs and sortable columns, so you can click a column header to sort by weight, value or damage. It also adds the Mod Configuration menu. Press Escape, then choose Mod Configuration, and you will find the settings for the mods that have them, including a settings page for Skyrim Souls itself. MCM Helper is the support piece that makes the settings pages for mods like Precision, True Directional Movement and Better Third Person Selection show up there. SkyUI and MCM Helper only change your own screen, so there is nothing to sync.
Now looting, where we have three upgrades.

QuickLoot changes containers. In ordinary Skyrim, opening a chest or a body means a full menu takes over the screen. With QuickLoot, you simply look at the container, and a small list of its contents appears beside it. By default, press E to take the highlighted item, or R to take everything. Whether items taken this way always match on your friends' screens has not been tested in multiplayer, so be a little careful with shared chests.

Better Third Person Selection changes how you pick things up when you play in third person. Ordinarily you have to line up a tiny marker on an item. With this mod, objects near you highlight as you walk up, and you press E on the item, door or body. It changes what you can select. It does not change who owns what is inside.

moreHUD adds information when you look at things. You can see whether you already know an item's enchantment, whether you have read a book, and the item's value and weight. That makes deciding what to carry much faster, which matters when the world will not wait while you decide.

Now supplies. Hunger and thirst are on in our game. They come on about thirty real minutes after you last ate or drank, and each one halves your health, magicka and stamina regeneration. Food clears Hunger, and a potion clears Thirst. So carry some food and a few potions, and put them in your favorites.
Now the big question: what belongs to whom?

Start with gold. Early on it comes the usual ways: loot from dungeons, bodies and containers, selling to vendors, and quest rewards. Coin purses hold anywhere from six to fifty-six gold, depending on their size. Each player has their own purse, and nothing is pooled. Dying costs no gold, because the server is set to take none. If you sell a piece of loot, the coins go to whoever sold it.

The world is different. Chests and bodies are one shared pile, and all four of you can take from them. So loot is split by who grabs it, not multiplied by four. If one player takes a sword from a bandit, it is gone for the others. That follows from how Skyrim Together shares containers, and nobody has watched it happen in our exact setup, so the honest advice is this: agree before you start who takes what, or accept that quick fingers win.

The Skyrim Together wiki says the contents of chests are synced, and several players can look at the same chest and take from it. As the server is set, things dropped on the ground are not shared, and the Skyrim Together wiki says another player picking one up does not sync either. So never use the floor to give something to a friend.

Vendors need a word. In ordinary Skyrim, early shopkeepers in Whiterun and Riverwood start with roughly five hundred to a thousand gold each, and their gold refreshes on a timer. Whether four players share one vendor's gold, or each see their own, has not been confirmed. If it is shared, four people's loot will empty a shop fast. Blacksmiths, jewelers and general-goods vendors will buy ore and ingots, and ordinary vendors will not buy stolen goods unless you have the Fence perk. Also remember that no one in Skyrim Together can sleep or wait time forward, so you cannot wait out a restock.

Next, your quest rewards. As episode three said, the party leader's game runs the important conversations. The leader's quest progress is copied to everyone, so all four journals move together. Who receives a reward, whether gold or an item, has not been tested in multiplayer. It is a thing to watch at the first hand-in.
Now handing things over.

There is no built-in trade window. The route that should work is a chest out in the world, not in a house. One player puts the item in, closes the chest, and the other takes it out. Try one plain item first, then ten gold.

Two more routes are less certain. The wiki lists pickpocketing another player as something that syncs, but a report from twenty twenty-two said it stopped working after an update, and nobody has confirmed how it behaves now. And finished potions and custom enchantments are the risky items: one report says a player-made potion could not be shared, and another said a custom enchantment arrived as the plain item. The wiki says enchanted and poisoned items sync, and the reports disagree with each other, so treat all of it as not yet tested in multiplayer. The safe habit is to craft for yourself and pass raw ingredients and ore around instead. Gear from the optional robes, hats and Lord of the Rings weapon mods is another case. A friend without those mods will not see it, and handing it over is untested.
Now homes.

As the server is set, the chests in the base game's homes are not synced, and that includes the homes from the expansions. What one player puts in a house chest is private to that player, so another player will not see it. That makes a house a good place for your own things, and a bad place to leave a delivery for a friend. Use a chest in the open world for hand-overs.

Finally, buying a house. In ordinary Skyrim, you can buy Breezehome in Whiterun for five thousand gold once you have completed the Bleak Falls Barrow quest. How buying a house works for four people at once has not been tested in multiplayer, so decide as a group who is buying and what you will do with it before anyone spends the gold.
One last habit. Each player keeps their own saves on their own computer. The server does not store your character for you, so save before you quit.

So, put together. Your menus do not pause, so get ready before the fight. Looting is quick, but the pile is shared, so agree who takes what. Your gold is yours. Hand things over through a world chest, never the floor, and never a house chest. And keep your crafted goods for yourself until the group has tested them.
That is the end of this episode.

episodes.title: Builds off the beaten path
episodes.summary: Character ideas that struggle alone but shine with friends, and why a group changes the math on Master difficulty.
transcript: This episode is for everyone who is still deciding who to be. It is about characters that might struggle if they played alone, but come into their own with friends. It makes sense after episodes one to five. Every idea here is a suggestion, not a class. Any race can learn any skill, and you can mix these freely.
Start with why a group changes the math.

As the server is set, the difficulty is Master. In plain terms, enemies take half the damage you deal, and you take double the damage they deal. That is the same for everyone, and enemies do not get stronger because more players have joined. Here is some simple arithmetic, not something anyone has watched happen. Four players all hitting one monster add their damage together, so the fight ends faster. A full, coordinated party faces roughly the same pressure as one person on ordinary difficulty. But one person alone on Master has a much harder time, and a character who deals little damage has the hardest time of all.

That is the opening for characters built around other people. A healer, a controller, a support caster and a talker are all weaker alone than they are in a party, and in a party they can be the reason everyone is still standing. A word of honesty about every build here: anything that depends on another player receiving your effect has not yet been tested in multiplayer.
Now, what the three big mods open up.

Mysticism reworks spells in every school and adds many new ones. Heal Other becomes an Apprentice spell, so a healer can look after friends from early on. Paralysis moves from Alteration into Illusion. Better Vanilla Perks keeps the shape of the perk trees but rewrites what the perks do, so familiar names may do new things. Imperious replaces each race's package with a different one, as episode five explained. Together they let you build characters that the ordinary game never really supported.
Here are the builds.

The healer. The idea is to keep everyone standing. The skills are Restoration first, then Alteration or one armor type, and a cheap way to fight back. A Breton or an Imperial suits it, but any race works. Mysticism gives a healer Heal Other, then Close Greater Wounds at Adept level, and then area heals called Breath of Life and Stendarr's Mercy. Grand Healing is channelled in Mysticism, not a single burst, so hold the cast. Better Vanilla Perks gives each Restoration cost-saving perk a magicka regeneration effect that grows as you climb, which suits long fights.

How to play it. Stand behind the frontline and slightly to one side. Aim heals by hand, because lock-on cannot select a friend. Keep enough magicka for one rescue heal. A few cautions. Do not build around the perk called Resurgence and its thirty percent bonus until it has been measured. And healing other players goes through a path that Skyrim Together supports, but our exact spells, amounts and experience gain have not yet been tested in multiplayer. Also, there is no resurrection spell that a healer can cast on a fallen friend. As the server is set, its death system gets a fallen player back on their feet by itself, and how that feels in our party has not been tested in multiplayer.

The paladin. The idea is a healer who can also hold the line. The skills are One Handed, Block, Restoration and Heavy Armor. Mysticism's Sunbeam, and the Sun Fire spell from the base game, give light-based attacks against the undead. As episode four said, Mortal Enemies makes enemies commit to their swings, so a shield fighter can read the wind-up. For a paladin, that commitment is the moment to cast. Casting a heal means taking a hand off your shield, so call "cover my cast" and let a friend step in.

The necromancer-healer. The idea is to keep the living alive while a conjured helper holds the enemy off. The skills are Restoration first, Conjuration second, and one defense. Mysticism adds Conjure Skeleton and Conjure Skeleton Archer, and familiar and atronach spells fill the early helper role. These are conjured creatures, not corpses raised from the floor. Place the helper to one side and leave the escape lane clear. Budget your magicka for both the summon and a rescue heal. And let the summon expire rather than spend your healing reserve to recast it. The group's budget is one controlled summon per player, and raising dead bodies is held. The full list of holds is in episode three.

The death knight. A heavy fighter with a dark helper. The skills are Two Handed and Heavy Armor, with a little Conjuration. A Nord or Orc fits well. Summon before you commit, then fight with your weapon. Frost magic or a health-draining enchantment adds flavor. This build does not heal the group, so someone else needs to cover that job.

The grey wizard. The idea is a travelling spellcaster with damage, protection and backup healing. The skills are Destruction and Alteration, then some Restoration. A Breton or a High Elf fits the theme. Bretons lose some reliable magic defense. High Elves start with less magicka than in the ordinary game, but revision seven helps here, because our own small patch gives High Elves Highborn back, the power they have in ordinary Skyrim. We tested it in single-player on October fourth. Mysticism's Destruction adds health-stealing spells such as Vampiric Touch, and Alteration adds Corrode Armor, which weakens an enemy before a friend hits it. Carry a second damage type for enemies that resist fire. A ward protects you, but whether it shields a friend is not yet tested in multiplayer.

The controller. The idea is to change what enemies can do instead of hitting the hardest. The skills are Illusion and Alteration, plus one reliable attack. Any race works. Mysticism expands control spells and weakening effects, and the morale spells Courage, Rally and Call to Arms have a route in Skyrim Together's code that reaches other players, though their effect in our party is not yet tested in multiplayer. Call "leave that one" when you have an enemy under control, so your friends do not break it. And keep an answer ready for enemies that resist control.

The storyteller. The traveller who talks, trades and carries the story. The skills are Speech, Restoration and one weapon. An Imperial, a Breton or a Khajiit fits well. Better Vanilla Perks gives Speech more than prices, as episode nine explained. There is no music or bard spell system in our build, and the quest leader still speaks in shared quest dialogue. So this is a flavor of play, more than a toolkit.

The Redguard spellsword. A fast fighter who keeps moving. The skills are One Handed, Light Armor and Destruction. Redguards gain momentum from humanoid kills and never run out of stamina outside combat. In revision seven, Redguards also have Adrenaline Rush back, the stamina power they have in ordinary Skyrim, thanks to the same patch. We tested that in single-player on October fourth. Redguards' other racial power is held.

The artisan. This one may surprise you. In our party, only combat experience is shared. Alchemy, Smithing and Enchanting level only for the player who does the crafting, so one person doing all the crafting levels the craft fastest. Better Vanilla Perks gives every material its own smithing perk, an Arcane Blacksmith perk for improving magical gear, strong Enchanter ranks, and the alchemy perks. A High Elf is a natural enchanter, with stronger enchantments at the cost of weaker physical gear. An Orc goes the other way. The risk is the hand-over. Passing finished custom potions and enchanted gear to a friend has not been tested in multiplayer, so craft for yourself first and share raw materials.
Last, the pairings.

A guardian and a healer benefit from predictable positioning. The guardian holds a corner, and the healer stands behind it. A guardian and a ranger divide the target jobs: one holds the melee while the other removes the archer or caster. A paladin and a wizard need explicit healing cover, so agree on who heals while the paladin is busy blocking. A necromancer-healer with a frontline needs clear summon placement, so the helper takes one flank and the exit stays empty.

One reminder for every build. Read perk and spell descriptions, but do not treat them as measured results. Stendarr's Aura says ten damage, while its underlying damage spell stores eight, and the real damage is unverified. Race bonuses come with losses too. The best character is the one you want to play for a whole campaign.
That is the end of this episode.

episodes.title: What to go looking for
episodes.summary: A short shopping list of spells, racial goals, perks and revision 7 additions worth hunting for because they are new or work differently.
transcript: This is a short episode for everyone, and it can wait until after your first night. It makes sense after episodes one to five. It is a shopping list of things in our game that are worth hunting for, because they are new, or because they work differently from the Skyrim you remember.
Start with spells.
